tracks.title: Push and pray
tracks.text: Lesson 08 point 7 — upgrades. A sub-lesson, under workflows. Push and pray. Picture a workflow that's already live. It's scheduled… it writes a report every night… and somewhere, a second workbook reads that report's output. Then you edit the plan — rename a field, change a type, drop a component you thought nobody used — and you redeploy. The break doesn't show up in your editor. [sighs] It shows up later… at the far end… when the consumer parses an output that no longer exists. Every platform answers this the same way — with process. Versioning policy. A changelog. A staging environment. A human, promising to be careful. All of it is people agreeing to remember a thing a machine could simply check. [curious] And that's the claim of this lesson. Compatibility of a plan's surface is not a matter of discipline. It's a computable fact. And if it's computable… a kernel can answer it before the deploy. Will this redeploy break a promise the old plan made?

tracks.title: The upgrade gate
tracks.text: So — the upgrade gate. The definition. It's a diff of a deployed plan's signature against a new one. Where exports may grow but never shrink. Imports may shrink but never grow. And a component's output type may never change. Empty diagnostics means the upgrade is safe. Anything else is a named, scoped list of promises about to break. Under the hood it's one pure function in the kernel — check upgrade, of old and new. It takes two org sources, parses each into per-workflow signatures, and returns a list of diagnostics. Its whole question, in one line — does everything the old plan promised still hold? Now, there are seven kinds of change it can judge, and the verdicts split cleanly. First… you add an export — safe. New consumers become possible, old ones untouched. Second… you remove an export — error. Someone downstream may be reading it. Third… you require a new import — a warn, not an error. It's a capability ask, and granting it is the engine's call. Fourth… a component's output type changes — error. Every consumer parses exactly that type. Fifth… you remove a whole workflow — error. Pruning it takes its exports with it. And here are the two most people miss. Sixth… you add a brand-new workflow — safe. The old plan promised nothing about it. And seventh… you remove an import, demanding less — also safe. [curious] And those last two aren't an oversight. The gate iterates the old workflows only. A workflow that exists only in the new plan is never even visited. And a dropped import is the absence of a thing the loop looks for. The gate doesn't ask whether the plan changed. It asks whether the old plan's promises survived.

tracks.title: Give grows, demand shrinks
tracks.text: Give grows… demand shrinks. The three rules point in opposite directions, and that's the whole idea. What a plan gives — its exports — may grow but never shrink. What a plan demands — its imports, its capabilities — may shrink but never grow. And the output type, the contract on each given thing, may not move at all. The reason is who depends on which. A consumer reads your exports, so taking one away breaks the consumer — adding one can't. A host grants your imports, so demanding a new one might exceed what the host will give — demanding fewer never does. [curious] Picture two boxes, the old plan and the new. In each one, two rows — the exports it gives, and the imports it demands. Now draw the arrows. On the exports row, left to right — add more — that arrow is green, always fine. On the imports row, right to left — demand fewer — green again, always fine. Then reverse each one. Drop an export… demand a new import… both arrows turn red. So you've got a one-way valve in each row, and the two valves face opposite directions. That opposition — exports one way, imports the other — is the entire safety property, drawn once.

tracks.title: The Motoko debt
tracks.text: The Motoko debt. These rules are borrowed, and the kernel says so in its own comments — the gate is labelled, job four, upgrade-compatibility gate, Motoko-style. The lineage is the Internet Computer. Canisters there are upgraded in place, and Candid — the platform's interface language — runs a service-subtype check that refuses an upgrade whose new interface isn't a structural subtype of the old. Same asymmetry. A service may offer more methods and demand less… never the reverse. And Motoko, the language, pairs that with stable variables — state declared to survive an upgrade. We borrow both. What we keep is the shape. What we simplify is everything underneath. Candid compares types through a real subtype lattice — a record with more fields is a subtype. Our kernel does no such thing. It compares output types as whole strings. So the analogy to Candid lives at the level of sets — which exports exist, which imports exist — not at the level of types. [curious] That's a deliberate floor… and the next sections are honest about where it sits.

tracks.title: One diff, three diagnostics
tracks.text: One diff… three diagnostics. The kernel ships a worked demo, and it runs end to end. Start with a one-component plan, version one. A workflow called Report, with a single component, Build. Build is written in rust, and its output is declared — report, of type string. Now version two changes exactly one line. Build starts emailing, so it adds a use of the net email capability… and its output flips from string to json. Run check upgrade on those two, and three diagnostics come back. First — an error. Export report-string removed, breaking. Second — a warn. New capability, net email, now required. Third — an error. Component Build, output type changed, breaking. One edit… three findings. And the double-count is honest, not a bug. Changing report-string to report-json is at the same time an export removal — the old export is gone — and an output-type change on Build. Both fire because both audiences are real. Whoever consumed the named export… and whoever parsed Build's output type. And notice the middle one is the only warn in the set. The new email capability is something the plan now asks for — and whether to grant it is the engine's decision, not the gate's. [curious] Here's the order the kernel works in. The caller hands in two org sources. The kernel computes a signature for the old plan, and a signature for the new — each a map keyed by workflow title. Then it walks the old map, and only the old map, in three passes. Pass one — anything the old plan exported that the new one doesn't. Pass two — every import the new plan added that the old one lacked. Pass three — every component whose output type differs. Each failure becomes one diagnostic, scoped to the workflow Report. The result is data… not an exception. What the caller does with it is the next question.

tracks.title: What gets compared
tracks.text: What gets compared. This one's a depth rung — skippable, but worth it. The thing being diffed is a signature — one per workflow — and two facts about it decide the gate's whole character. First… signatures are keyed by workflow title. The map the diff reads from uses the workflow's headline text as its key. That's why a rename reads as a break. Change Report to Summary, and the old Report is simply missing from the new map — removed — while Summary is a stranger the old plan never promised. Two workflows that share a title collide in the map, last one wins. Title is identity here. Second… signatures are computed flat. A workflow's signature is taken over every component descendant — walking past intervening sub-workflows, collecting them all. That's the opposite of the lens the compiled plan uses, which scopes each world to its direct children for execution. Same tree, two readings — scoped for running… flat for the safety diff. And the flat reading is deliberate. A parent answers for the promises of its sub-worlds. Now, the signature holds four fields. Imports — the deduped union of every component's uses. Exports — every output not consumed by another component inside the world. Component-outputs — a map from each component name to its declared type. And edges — the wiring between components, computed but read by no rule. [curious] The export one is the subtle one. An output is an export only if nothing else inside the same world consumes it. Wire one component's output into another's input, and that value stops being a promise to the outside — it's internal plumbing now. Consumption is encapsulation. Hold onto that… it sets a trap in a moment.

tracks.title: What the gate cannot see
tracks.text: What the gate cannot see. Another depth rung. The gate diffs a plan's surface — and only its surface. That word is load-bearing. Everything below the surface is invisible to it, because the loop only iterates old workflows and only inspects four fields. So here's the honest list of what a clean diff does not promise. You rewrote a component's whole source body — not caught. The gate never reads the implementation. You switched a component from rust to javascript — not caught. Language isn't in the signature. You changed its dependencies — not caught. You rewired the edges between components — not caught. You changed the schedule — not caught. You removed a component whose output was internal — not caught, because a consumed output was never an export. And you added a brand-new component — not caught, because new things break no old promise. The one thing in that list it does catch — changing an output type, report-string to report-json. [curious] And two cautions follow. First, that type check is string equality. Full stop. The strings differ, so it trips — there's no notion that one type widens or narrows another. A type that's genuinely compatible but spelled differently still fails. A type spelled the same but meaning something new sails right through. And second, the bigger one — surface is not behavior. A component can keep every export, every type, every import… and have its body rewritten to do the exact opposite of what it did. The gate sees nothing. It's the same line the grammar draws everywhere — structure is checkable, logic is not. The gate polices the contract… never the conduct behind it.

tracks.title: The state that crosses
tracks.text: The state that crosses. A gate that approves a redeploy is only half the question. The other half is what survives it. When the new plan replaces the old, components are torn down and re-instantiated — they're stateless between runs, by design. So what about the component that was holding something worth keeping? That's the second Motoko borrowing. Persist. The same idea as stable variables, at the same plan granularity. Persist is a bare flag in a component's header — no value, just the word. It parses into the plan as a boolean per component, and a runtime function — durable components — walks the plan, worlds and nested sub-workflows, recursively, and returns the names that declared it. Picture the demo. A workflow called Agent, with two components. Remember, written in rust — it declares persist, and outputs a memory in json. And Act, written in javascript — it takes that memory as input. Call durable components on that plan, and you get back a one-element list — just Remember. Remember opted into durability. Act consumes its memory but declares nothing of its own. [curious] Now the part people get wrong. Persist is not a memory snapshot. The state doesn't live in raw linear memory the runtime freezes and thaws. It lives in the V-F-S — the workbook's own SQLite-backed disk. Persist is the contract that a component checkpoints its state into that disk, rather than relying on a memory image. Picture the hand-off. The old Remember instance checkpoints its state into a memory volume that persists… and throws its scratch into a tmp volume. The gate approves the swap. The new Remember instance resumes — and memory and workspace come back, while tmp is gone. The machinery underneath is real. Freeze copies the SQLite file to cold storage. Resume copies it back, clearing tmp while memory and workspace persist. And Litestream replicates the file off-box. The flag is just how the runtime knows who to carry across.

tracks.title: A gate with no hands
tracks.text: A gate with no hands. One last depth rung, and it closes the loop. Check upgrade is a pure component — its whole world is string-in, string-out, with no host imports and no system context at all. It can't touch a disk. Can't open a socket. Can't refuse anything. A fault inside it traps within the runtime and goes nowhere. It is a function that computes a verdict and hands it back… and that is all it can do. And that purity is exactly why it travels. The same logic is linked natively into the command-line tool as a plain rust function, and embedded into the runtime as a compiled component loaded at startup. One logic… two surfaces… with no separate wasm version of the rule. [curious] And it's why refusing is necessarily the caller's job. A gate with no hands can't stop a deploy. It can only tell the truth about it. Whoever holds the deploy path reads the diagnostics, and decides. The gate that polices every component's surface is itself a typed component — it rides the very model it imposes.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Where it bites. The honesty section — and the most important one. This lesson describes a gate that exists… and wiring it is something we're still waiting on. So do not hear any of this as a promise that your redeploys are gated today. They aren't yet. Here's the exact ledger. Callable today — the kernel export, check upgrade, and the demo that drives it. You can reproduce every diagnostic in this lesson in a live session right now. Not wired — no deploy path calls check upgrade. The command-line tool exposes query, tangle, and lint — there is no check-upgrade verb. The web and socket dispatchers expose tangle and validate only. Nothing stops at the gate on its way to production. It's a kernel export with a runtime wrapper. Turning it into a tollbooth is the runtime's job — not yet done. And persistence is the same status. Durable components is also called only by the demo. The plan carries the persist flag, the runtime can enumerate who set it, but the run path doesn't yet checkpoint on anyone's behalf automatically. Enumerable today… not auto-enforced. And two sharp edges in the gate as written. Renames read as remove-plus-add, because title is identity. And two same-titled workflows collide in the signature map, last write wins. [curious] These are boundaries of the current design — stated as boundaries… not apologies.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is this just semver? No. Semver is a promise a human makes by hand — they decide whether a change is major and write a number. This is a diff a kernel computes from the two plans themselves. No judgment to forget, no number to get wrong. Why is a new import only a warn? Because it's a request, not a break. The plan is asking for a capability it didn't ask for before — and whether to grant that is the engine's call, not the gate's. What if I rename a workflow? The gate reads it as removing the old one and adding a new one — breaking. Signatures are keyed by title, so the title is the identity. A rename and a real delete-plus-create look identical to the diff. Does persist snapshot my memory? No. Components are stateless on every start, so there's no live image to snapshot. Persist is the contract that the component checkpoints into the V-F-S — the workbook's disk — which the runtime freezes and resumes. Can I run the gate today? You can call it — and the demo runs every example here. What you can't do today is have it automatically stop a deploy. No deploy path consults it yet. And — does it check that my code actually changed? [chuckles] No. It diffs the surface — exports, imports, output types, by title. It never reads a component's body. You can rewrite a component to do the opposite of what it did, and as long as the surface holds, the gate returns empty. Surface compatibility is not behavioral verification.

tracks.title: Back up to workflows
tracks.text: So that's the upgrade gate. Not process… not a promise to be careful. A diff a kernel computes — exports may grow but never shrink, imports may shrink but never grow, output types frozen — and a named list of what you're about to break, before anything runs. [curious] The way back up is short. This sub-lesson sits under workflows — lesson eight — the plan this gate guards. The composition half of it — grafting and pruning whole subtrees — lives in the nesting lesson. And the substrate where persist state actually survives is the V-F-S. Three doors… all of them one step away.
